content: 1. The need for additional analgesia at six hours post-administration is reduced when compared to placebo, but the evidence supporting this is of very low certainty. 2. It is unclear whether a single dose of any NSAID, regardless of dosage, affects the risk of adverse effects at four hours post-administration compared to placebo, as the evidence is of very low certainty. 3. Subgroup analyses based on the type and dose of NSAIDs yielded the following findings: It is uncertain whether a single dose of ibuprofen (300–400 mg or 900 mg), ketoprofen (25 mg or 50 mg), aceclofenac (50 mg, 100 mg, or 150 mg), diflunisal (125 mg, 250 mg, or 500 mg), antrafenine (300 mg), or flurbiprofen (25 mg, 50 mg, or 100 mg) affects the risk of adverse effects at six hours post-administration compared to placebo. The evidence is of very low certainty. 4. Maternal functioning, well-being, and experiences of postnatal care were not reported in any of the trials included in the three systematic reviews. 5. Newborn outcomes, including breastfeeding status and adverse effects, were not reported in the included trials. 6. When comparing a single dose of aspirin to a higher single dose of aspirin: It is uncertain whether any dose of aspirin (300 mg or 600 mg) improves pain relief as reported by women compared to a higher dose of aspirin (600 mg or 1200 mg). The evidence is of very low certainty. It is unclear whether any dose of aspirin (300 mg or 600 mg) reduces the need for additional perineal pain relief compared to a higher dose of aspirin (600 mg or 1200 mg). The evidence is of very low certainty. It is uncertain whether any dose of aspirin affects the risk of adverse effects compared to a higher dose of aspirin. The evidence is of very low certainty. 7. When comparing a single dose of NSAIDs to a higher single dose of the same NSAID: It is uncertain whether any dose of the following NSAIDs improves pain relief at four and/or six hours post-administration compared to a higher dose of the same NSAID: ibuprofen (300–400 mg vs. 800 mg), diclofenac (25 mg vs. 50 mg or 100 mg), diflunisal (125 mg or 250 mg vs. 250 mg or 500 mg), ketoprofen (25 mg vs. 50 mg), aceclofenac (50 mg or 100 mg vs. 150 mg), etodolac (25 mg vs. 100 mg), flurbiprofen (25 mg or 50 mg vs. 50 mg or 100 mg), and fenoprofen (any dose vs. any higher dose). The evidence is of very low certainty. It is unclear whether any dose of the above NSAIDs reduces the need for additional pain relief at four and/or six hours post-administration compared to a higher dose of the same NSAID. The evidence is of very low certainty. It is uncertain whether any dose of the above NSAIDs affects the risk of adverse effects at four and/or six hours post-administration compared to a higher dose of the same NSAID. The evidence is of very low certainty. 8. Aceclofenac (100 mg) versus paracetamol (650 mg): It is uncertain whether aceclofenac (100 mg) provides adequate pain relief at four or six hours post-administration compared to paracetamol (650 mg). The evidence is of very low certainty. It is unclear whether aceclofenac (100 mg) affects the risk of adverse effects at six hours post-administration compared to paracetamol (650 mg). The evidence is of very low certainty. 9. Aspirin (900 mg) versus ibuprofen: It is uncertain whether aspirin (900 mg) provides adequate pain relief at six hours post-administration compared to ibuprofen (300–400 mg or 900 mg). The evidence is of very low certainty. 10. Aspirin (500–650 mg) versus other NSAIDs: It is unclear whether aspirin (500–650 mg) provides adequate pain relief at four and six hours post-administration compared to diflunisal (125 mg, 250 mg, or 500 mg), ibuprofen (300–400 mg), diclofenac (25 mg, 50 mg, or 100 mg), or flurbiprofen (25 mg, 50 mg, or 100 mg). The evidence is of very low certainty. It is uncertain whether aspirin (500–650 mg or 900 mg) reduces the need for additional analgesia at four or six hours post-administration compared to other NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, flurbiprofen). The evidence is of very low certainty. It is unclear whether aspirin (500–650 mg or 900 mg) increases the risk of adverse effects at four and six hours post-administration compared to other NSAIDs (e.g., dipyrone, flurbiprofen, diflunisal, ibuprofen). The evidence is of very low certainty. 11. Pharmacological interventions for postpartum perineal pain relief: Other forms of pharmacological pain relief, such as rectal analgesics and topical anesthetics, were not considered in the included trials. No economic evaluations of pharmacological treatments for perineal pain relief were identified. Pharmacological interventions may increase equity as they are widely available without a prescription and at low cost. However, equity may decrease if women are expected to pay for analgesics themselves. 12. Paracetamol is considered safe during breastfeeding. Although a single case of a rash in a breastfeeding infant has been reported, the American Academy of Pediatrics considers paracetamol compatible with breastfeeding. No other adverse effects of paracetamol exposure through breast milk have been reported. Following maternal treatment with 1000 mg of paracetamol, the maximum dose an infant is exposed to is estimated to be less than 2% of the maternal dose. 13. Aspirin is contraindicated during breastfeeding due to evidence of potentially harmful effects on breastfeeding infants from salicylate and its metabolites excreted in breast milk. 14. The use of opioids for uterine cramping pain relief is discouraged as they show no advantage over NSAIDs, are associated with maternal adverse effects, are contraindicated during breastfeeding, and carry a risk of psychological and physical dependence. 15. Women should be informed about uterine involution and changes in lochia postpartum. They should be asked about abdominal pain and vaginal discharge during their postpartum stay in health facilities and at each postnatal care contact. Women should also be advised of danger signs and symptoms, including exacerbation of uterine pain, which may indicate postpartum complications such as endometritis.
